headline: Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo returns to Riyadh for a third edition
deck: The organisers put the show at more than 170 exhibitors and 3,500 products, across a floor that now runs from pallet racking to autonomous handling.
excerpt: The third Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo opens at the Riyadh International Convention & Exhibition Center on 8 September, with more than 170 local and international exhibitors showing over 3,500 products and services across warehousing, cold chain, freight, fleet and terminals.
content:
The third edition of the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo opens at the Riyadh International Convention & Exhibition Center on 8 September and runs to the 10th. The organisers say more than 170 local and international exhibitors will show over 3,500 products and services.

The declared scope runs across warehousing and storage, cargo, cold chain, freight forwarding, last-mile delivery, e-commerce fulfilment, fleet and commercial vehicles, multimodal transport, ports and terminals, and third-party logistics. Exhibitors named by the organisers include SAL Logistics, MS Logistics, Al Dress, Swisslog, SSI Schäfer, JAL, Ajlan, Kardex and Sadr Logistics.

That exhibitor list is a reasonable map of where the Saudi logistics market currently sits. It pairs national operators — SAL, Sadr, Ajlan — with European materials handling and automation manufacturers whose products are the capital equipment inside a modern distribution centre. Swisslog, SSI Schäfer and Kardex do not sell logistics services; they sell racking, shuttles, cranes, sortation and the software that co-ordinates them. Their presence at a Riyadh show in volume is itself the signal.

The demand behind it is a policy programme with numbers attached. Saudi Arabia's National Transport and Logistics Strategy has committed substantial capital to multimodal freight infrastructure, targets 59 logistics zones by 2030, and sets an objective for the logistics sector to contribute 10 per cent of gross domestic product. More than 100 million square metres of logistics-zone area is planned, distributed to give access to both coasts.

Underneath the policy is a market that has been growing without needing it. Third-party logistics warehousing in the Kingdom is estimated at around $3.74bn in 2026, forecast to reach $4.94bn by 2031. The growth driver is not only the construction programme but the shift in how goods reach consumers: e-commerce fulfilment imposes storage, picking and delivery requirements that a traditional distribution warehouse was never built to meet.

What a visitor should watch for on the floor is the split between two kinds of purchase. The first is capacity — racking, shelving, forklifts, dock equipment, the fabric of a warehouse. That market grows with square metres and is well served. The second is throughput — automated storage and retrieval, shuttle systems, goods-to-person picking, sortation and the control software above them. That market grows with labour cost, order profile and land price rather than with floor area, and it is the one whose economics in Saudi Arabia are still being worked out.

Automation displaces labour, and it is justified where labour is expensive, scarce or unreliable, or where land constraints make height cheaper than footprint. Which of those conditions holds in Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province, and for which categories of goods, is exactly the calculation the buyers walking this floor are running.

The show runs at RICEC from 3pm daily until 10 September.
